blocks.title: What is this file?
blocks.what: A Service gives Pods one stable address. It comes from the core v1 API.
blocks.why: This one asks AWS for a load balancer, so people outside the cluster can reach your app.
blocks.ifRemoved: Kubernetes rejects the file, because it cannot tell what you want to create.
blocks.comment: What to create: a Service, from the core v1 API

blocks.title: Give it a name
blocks.why: Auto Mode also uses the name when it names the AWS load balancer.
blocks.ifRemoved: Kubernetes rejects the file, because every object needs a name.
blocks.comment: A name to find the Service
blocks.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-public

blocks.title: Make it public
blocks.what: An annotation is a note that other tools read. This one asks for an internet-facing load balancer.
blocks.why: Auto Mode makes an internal load balancer unless you ask, so only your VPC could reach it.
blocks.ifRemoved: Auto Mode creates an internal load balancer. Your laptop cannot reach it.
blocks.comment: Ask AWS for a load balancer that the internet can reach
blocks.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-public
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: internet-facing

blocks.title: Ask for a load balancer
blocks.what: type: LoadBalancer asks for an outside address. loadBalancerClass names who provides it: Auto Mode’s Network Load Balancer.
blocks.why: On an Auto Mode cluster, eks.amazonaws.com/nlb is already the default. Writing it makes the file clear.
blocks.ifRemoved: Without type, the Service is a ClusterIP Service, reachable only inside the cluster.
blocks.comment: An AWS Network Load Balancer, created by EKS Auto Mode
blocks.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-public
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: internet-facing
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  loadBalancerClass: eks.amazonaws.com/nlb

blocks.title: Which Pods get traffic?
blocks.what: The selector sends traffic to Pods labelled app: web, from the Deployment lesson.
blocks.why: The load balancer forwards to these Pods, wherever they run.
blocks.ifRemoved: The Service has no Pods, so the load balancer has nowhere to send traffic.
blocks.comment: Send traffic to Pods labelled app: web
blocks.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-public
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: internet-facing
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  loadBalancerClass: eks.amazonaws.com/nlb
  selector:
    app: web

blocks.title: Which port?
blocks.what: Listen on port 80 and forward to port 80 in each Pod. This block makes the file ready.
blocks.why: nginx listens on port 80 inside its container.
blocks.ifRemoved: Kubernetes rejects the Service, because it must say which port to listen on.
blocks.comment: Port 80 on the load balancer goes to port 80 in the Pods
blocks.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-public
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: internet-facing
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  loadBalancerClass: eks.amazonaws.com/nlb
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 80

notes.apiVersion: The API group and version. Services are in the core v1 API.
notes.metadata: Details that identify the object, such as its name.
notes.kind: The type of object to create. A Service gives Pods one stable address.
notes.metadata.name: The Service name. kubectl get service web-public shows its outside address.
notes.metadata.annotations: Notes for other tools. Auto Mode reads these to configure the load balancer.
notes.metadata.annotations.service.beta.kubern: internet-facing: anyone on the internet can reach it. The default, internal, allows only your VPC.
notes.spec: The desired state: what kind of Service, which Pods, which ports.
notes.spec.type: LoadBalancer: ask the cloud for a load balancer with an outside address.
notes.spec.loadBalancerClass: Who provides the load balancer: EKS Auto Mode’s Network Load Balancer. It cannot change later.
notes.spec.selector: Pods with all of these labels receive traffic.
notes.spec.selector.app: Send traffic to Pods labelled app: web, from the Deployment lesson.
notes.spec.ports: The ports the Service listens on. Each list item is one port.
notes.spec.ports[].port: The load balancer listens on port 80.
notes.spec.ports[].targetPort: Traffic goes to port 80 inside each Pod, where nginx listens.

tryIt.result: Starts the two nginx Pods from the Deployment lesson.
Prints service/web-public created. Auto Mode starts creating a Network Load Balancer.
EXTERNAL-IP shows a name ending in amazonaws.com after a minute or two.
Prints the nginx welcome page from your laptop. A new name can take a few minutes to work.
Removes the Service. Auto Mode deletes the load balancer too, which stops its charges.
Removes the Deployment and its Pods.

questions.question: Without the scheme annotation, who can reach the load balancer?
questions.explain: Auto Mode makes an internal load balancer by default. internet-facing makes it public.

questions.question: Who creates the AWS load balancer?
answers: EKS Auto Mode, named by loadBalancerClass
questions.explain: Auto Mode watches for LoadBalancer Services of its class and creates the load balancer for you.

questions.question: Which Pods receive the traffic?
questions.explain: The selector picks Pods by label, as for every Service.

fix.command: aws elbv2 describe-load-balancers --query "LoadBalancers[?DNSName=='$(kubectl get service web-public -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].hostname}')'].Scheme" --output text
fix.explain: The annotation says schema, not scheme. Auto Mode ignores the unknown annotation, so AWS makes an internal load balancer your laptop cannot reach.

sources.title: Use Service annotations to configure Network Load Balancers
